name: Melanocytic Nevi
overview: Melanocytic Nevi, commonly known as moles, are benign collections of melanocytes (pigment-producing cells) within the skin. They are among the most common skin lesions, with most adults having multiple nevi. The majority remain stable throughout life and never become cancerous. However, because melanoma may occasionally develop within or resemble a mole, regular skin monitoring is recommended.
description: Melanocytic nevi usually appear as well-defined brown, tan, or skin-colored spots or raised lesions. They may be present from birth or develop during childhood and early adulthood. Most remain unchanged for many years, although slight changes in size or pigmentation can occur with aging. Clinical evaluation is recommended if a mole develops suspicious features or changes over time.
clinical_presentation: May occur anywhere on the body

ABCDE.Color: Uniform brown, tan, black, or skin-colored.
ABCDE.Diameter: Usually less than 6 mm, although benign larger nevi can occur.
ABCDE.Evolution: Stable over time. Any noticeable change should be evaluated.

risk_factors: Large number of nevi on the body
diagnostic_workup: Skin biopsy if suspicious changes are present
treatment_options: No treatment required for typical benign nevi
Surgical excision if suspicious changes develop
Removal for cosmetic reasons after medical consultation
prognosis: The prognosis is excellent. Most melanocytic nevi remain benign throughout life. Regular skin monitoring helps detect uncommon but important changes that may require medical evaluation.
prevention: Attend regular dermatology check-ups if you have numerous or atypical moles
next_steps: Continue routine skin self-examinations using the ABCDE rule.
Schedule annual dermatology examinations if recommended.
Take photographs to monitor larger or atypical moles over time.
Seek medical evaluation if any mole develops significant changes.
red_flags: Multiple colors developing within the lesion
Formation of a new dark lesion in adulthood

follow_up.routine: Annual skin examination or as recommended by your dermatologist.
follow_up.high_risk: Individuals with numerous atypical nevi or a strong family history of melanoma may require more frequent surveillance.

patient_advice: Learn and regularly apply the ABCDE rule when examining your skin.
Take dated photographs of larger or unusual moles to monitor changes.
Avoid excessive sun exposure and tanning beds.
Consult a dermatologist promptly if a mole changes in size, shape, color, or symptoms.
medical_disclaimer: This information is intended for educational purposes only and does not replace professional medical evaluation. Most melanocytic nevi are benign; however, any changing skin lesion should be assessed by a qualified healthcare professional.
